claim: Gain vs loss wording of the same Asian disease problem flips majority choice between subjects (72% sure option in gain wording, 22% in loss, 1981). Many Labs 1: 62.2% vs 33.5% sure option, chi2(1)=516.41, N=6,271, d=.60, 36 samples; 47-country COVID survey N=88,181 d=0.69. The replication swing is about 29 points, not 50. (Many Labs 2 d=0.40 concerns a different Tversky and Kahneman 1981 problem, the discounted-item trip, and should not be cited here.)
agent_test: Run the same item in gain and loss wording N times each at equal tokens; compare cross-frame disagreement to same-wording repeat disagreement.
audit_note: ML1 (62.2% vs 33.5%, chi2=516.41, d=.60, 6344-73=6271) and Rachev (d=.69, N=88,181, 47 countries) check out, but the Many Labs 2 d=0.40 (N=7,228) is the trip/discount-item problem (Tversky and Kahneman 1981 mental accounting), not the Asian disease problem.
claim_before_audit: Gain vs loss wording of the same Asian disease problem flips majority choice between subjects (72% sure option in gain wording, 22% in loss, 1981). Many Labs 1 primary text: 62.2% vs 33.5% sure option, chi2(1)=516.41, N=6,271, d=.60, 36 samples, none reversed; Many Labs 2 d=0.40; 47-country N=88,181 d=0.69. The replication swing is about 29 points, not 50.

claim: Pooled human risky-choice framing effect is small to medium but reliable, not tiny: d 0.31 (Kuhberger 1998), 0.52 after p-curve correction for publication bias (Steiger and Kuhberger 2018), 0.437 (Pinon and Gambara 2005, 51 studies, 151 estimates, about 13,500 subjects), 0.56 (2016 studies), 0.60 (Many Labs 1). Heterogeneity is significant and attribute framing is smaller (0.26).
agent_test: Expect partial shifts, so use many wordings and runs; do not test with one item.
audit_note: All d values match (0.31, 0.52, 0.437, 0.56, 0.60, attribute 0.26; 51 studies, 151 estimates, ~13,500), but d of 0.3 to 0.6 is small-to-medium by Cohen's convention, not medium to large; Steiger and Kuhberger's 0.52 is the re-analysis of Kuhberger's data.
claim_before_audit: Pooled human risky-choice framing effect is medium to large, not tiny: d 0.31 (Kuhberger 1998), 0.52 after p-curve correction for publication bias (Steiger and Kuhberger 2018), 0.437 (Pinon and Gambara 2005, 51 studies, 151 estimates, about 13,500 subjects, full text read), 0.56 (2016 studies), 0.60 (Many Labs 1). Heterogeneity is very high and attribute framing is smaller (0.26).

claim: Seeing both wordings (within-subject) cuts the human effect by roughly two thirds (d 0.18 vs 0.50 between), and thoughtful people are more consistent only when both versions are visible; thoughtfulness alone gives no advantage.
agent_test: Compare single-wording answer vs answer after showing both wordings side by side, equal total tokens.
audit_note: Pinon and Gambara risky framing d=0.50 between vs 0.18 within (about 64% smaller); Kahneman 2003 and Broniatowski and Reyna support the thoughtfulness point (via LeBoeuf and Shafir).

claim: Cognitive style and numeracy do not reliably protect humans (Mandel and Kapler N=506, r=0.02-0.08); a numeracy moderator appears in one small study (Peters and Levin N=108, p=.05).
agent_test: Check whether a stronger or more deliberate model setting reduces the gap; do not assume it.

claim: The effect depends on option structure, not the words gain/loss: removing the stated zero outcome of the risky option removes it (57.22% vs 53.63%, N=1,119), removing the non-zero outcome roughly doubles it. Favours fuzzy-trace over prospect theory; a fuzzy-trace model predicted 93% of 88 pairs (proponent authors).
agent_test: Vary which complements are stated in the prompt and measure the flip rate.
audit_note: Zhou et al. 2021 Type 2 57.22% vs 53.63%, N=1119 (df 1113); Type 3 gap 45.8 vs 20.7 points for classic; Broniatowski and Reyna 82/88 (93%); 'favours fuzzy-trace' is the proponents' reading, as the claim notes.

claim: The 'at least 200' reading (Mandel 2014) does not explain the effect: adding 'exactly' leaves it intact in a larger replication, though Mandel disputes this.
agent_test: Test an 'exactly' clarification vs a full canonical restatement on the agent.

claim: Real money at small stakes does not remove the human effect (1981 paid version, N=126: 67% A, 86% D).
agent_test: State that stakes are real in the prompt and measure whether the flip changes.

claim: Context moderates the human effect: higher perceived stress and coronavirus concern went with a larger framing effect in the Disease problem (Rachev 2021, 88,181 participants); in a meta-analysis of 18 studies the age difference in risk taking depended on scenario (gain-framed small-amount financial and large-amount mortality items; loss-framed high-amount mortality items).
agent_test: Strip alarm and stakes language in the neutral rewrite and compare flip rates.
audit_note: Rachev supports stress and concern raising the framing effect; Best and Charness (18 studies) find the age effect in gain frames driven by small-amount financial AND large-amount mortality scenarios, plus a younger-riskier effect in loss-framed high-amount mortality scenarios, so 'only in gain frame for mortality content' is wrong; 'lives-at-stake strengthens it' is not shown by either paper and the Nakamura foreign-language source could not be opened (page returned only a title).
claim_before_audit: Domain and context moderate the human effect: lives-at-stake and alarm strengthen it (stress and concern interactions, Rachev), age effect only in gain frame for mortality content, foreign-language effect only partly replicates.

claim: LLMs reproduce the framing flip: GPT-3 chooses the risky option 60.0% of the time under the die framing vs 11.3% under the save framing for save probabilities below 0.5 (Jones and Steinhardt 2022); four 2025 models show 27-42% framing-violation rates on the Asian disease text (Puutio and Do, preprint); Payne 2025 five frontier models reach a framing effect of up to +1.84 on a 0-2 risk scale in some scenarios (others near zero or negative).
agent_test: Measure our model on classic and novel wordings; novel wordings avoid training-data memory.
audit_note: Jones and Steinhardt Table 9 gives GPT-3 risky choice of 60.0% (die) vs 11.3% (save) for save probabilities below 0.5; 21.9% is the 0.5 bin and 28/78 are the human 1981 figures. Puutio and Do (27-42% violation range) and Payne (+1.84 max, 5 models) check out.
claim_before_audit: LLMs reproduce the framing flip: GPT-3 near p=1/3 (60.0% risky under die vs about 22% under save), four 2025 models 27-42% reversal on the classic text, Payne 2025 five frontier models up to +1.84 on a 0-2 scale in some scenarios.

claim: LLM framing size varies strongly by scenario domain and even reverses sign (military/sport large, business near zero, career negative). Payne: 25 runs per cell; o3 significant in 4 of 7 scenarios, Claude-4-Thinking in 6 of 7. FrameBench: effect falls with probability level (risk shift 0.535 at 20% to 0.109 at 80%); no per-domain table found in its text.
agent_test: Test across at least four domains.

claim: Reasoning-trained models are nearly frame-invariant on explicit two-option money prospects (correlation with expected payoff 0.86-1.0, Ge et al.) and more frame-resistant on attribute templates (Knipper: QwQ-32B .818 vs Qwen2.5-32B .602), but on story scenarios they still flip beyond within-cell noise (Payne: o3 4 of 7, Claude-4-Thinking 6 of 7; FrameBench: GPT-5 33.4% category change vs 7.12% pooled repeat noise). The result depends on task format.
agent_test: Run both an explicit-prospect task and a story task on the agent's model.

claim: Rewriting input into a canonical form that states both complementary probabilities cuts LLM category change from 34.20% to 6.68% (near the 7.12% repeat-noise floor); an 'ignore the frame' instruction only reaches 22.83%. Full-text check (d10): the canonical form was one sentence giving both probabilities, not a code-run table; 3 models, 32 scenarios. Symbolic stripping plus forced EV calculation removed the effect completely in Payne's control (o3 200/200 indifferent).
agent_test: Implement code-run canonicalization and compare with an instruction-only arm at equal tokens.

claim: Awareness or generic debias instructions help little (CogBias +5.8 pp on framing, backfire on other biases; BiasBuster awareness no help for GPT-4; FrameBench instruction 22.83%) and chain-of-thought can raise flips in small models (28.6% to 57.1%). Echterhoff full text: GPT-4 awareness delta -0.470, contrastive -0.410, counterfactual -0.570 vs baseline -0.405 (no help). Counter-evidence: reasoning-trained 14-70B open models resist framing better than size-matched non-reasoning models (Knipper).
agent_test: Add an instruction-only arm and a CoT arm; measure flip rate.
audit_note: All numbers check (CogBias +5.8 framing with backfires on others, Echterhoff GPT-4 -0.470/-0.410/-0.570 vs -0.405, FRAGILE CoT 28.6 to 57.1, Knipper framing scores for reasoning models); minor: FrameBench frame-robust prompting cut category change from 34.20% to 22.83%, an 11-point drop that is partial rather than none.

claim: Model-written neutral rewrite (selfhelp) removed the GPT-4 admit/reject framing gap (-0.405 to -0.010; 2.7% of framing prompts remain biased) and cut GPT-3.5 to -0.080 (from +0.165); it worked for Llama-2 7B/13B on framing (1.4%/0% biased) but not for other biases in small models; alternative-framing-then-revise (DeFrame) cut framing disparity 92% on BBQ.
agent_test: Have the agent rewrite the prompt neutrally and check that all numbers were preserved; measure flip rate.
audit_note: Echterhoff Table values (-0.405 to -0.010; GPT-3.5 +0.165 to -0.080; 2.7% framing in GPT-4; Llama-2 1.4%/0%) and DeFrame 92% framing-disparity reduction on BBQ match.

claim: LLMs show modest loss aversion on described gambles (pooled lambda 1.26 across 32 models and 11 studies; below the strongest human estimate of 1.96 but compatible with more conservative human estimates of 1.07 and 1.31) and a human-like inverse-S probability weighting (on few studies); replacing numeric probabilities with verbal probability markers shifts LLM choices (Wang et al.).
agent_test: Use numeric probabilities in canonical form; do not model the agent as a human value function.
audit_note: Pooled lambda 1.26 (32 models, 11 studies) is right, but 1.96 is only the strongest human meta-analytic estimate; the paper says 1.26 is compatible with more conservative human estimates (1.07, 1.31), and probability weighting rests on few studies.
claim_before_audit: LLMs show weak human-style loss aversion on described gambles (pooled lambda 1.26 vs human 1.96, 32 models) but near-human probability weighting; verbal probability markers shift choices.

claim: Framing damage in LLMs accumulates across turns (evidence-direction agreement 78.4% vs 70.7% multi-turn) and stale or tool-description text can act as a frame.
agent_test: Re-derive the question neutrally each loop step and compare to carrying the original wording.

claim: Parallel agents sharing one wording share its bias: 82 models swing from 4.3% to 68.8% option B between two equivalent threshold-voting wordings. Full text: the 4.3% and 68.8% use all 1,640 responses per scenario as denominator, including 98 and 166 non-compliant ones (valid-only 4.5% and 76.5%); the task is a survival story with instrumental vs cooperative wording, not a gain-loss frame.
agent_test: Give vote members different canonical wordings and compare to same-wording sampling.

claim: Cognitive load amplifies the human effect after a demanding dialogue (h 0.205 ns vs 0.730, z 3.53, N=1,648). LLMs role-playing the participant with the same dialogue also show a larger effect in 2 of 3 prompt styles (1.770 to 2.447; 1.252 to 2.299; third prompt 0.690 to 0.810 ns), but this is persona prediction at 3 to 9 times the human size, not the agent's own judgment under long context, which is untested.
agent_test: Pad context with demanding text and measure the flip.

claim: Time pressure effect on framing is contested in humans (Svenson and Benson reduced it; Guo 2017 and Diederich 2018 amplified it) and unverified here.
agent_test: Vary token budget and measure flip rate.

claim: A symbolic rewrite with forced expected-value calculation removes the framing effect in strong models: o3 declared indifference in 200/200 trials in both frames, GPT-4o in 100% of its trials, while the same models showed large effects on the story version.
agent_test: Rewrite the problem into a final-state table (both complements), compute the numbers in code, then choose. Compare to a model-written neutral rewrite and a plain instruction at equal tokens.

claim: On story-format problems, reasoning-class models still flip beyond noise. Payne: o3 significant in 4 of 7 scenarios and Claude-4-Thinking in 6 of 7 (25 runs per cell, Mann-Whitney). FrameBench-HPS (4 domains): GPT-5 changed recommendation category in 33.40% of groups; pooled same-wording repeat disagreement was 7.12%. Model-specific noise and per-domain results were not reported.
agent_test: Measure the agent's own repeat noise on the same wording and compare with the cross-frame flip on at least four domains.
audit_note: Payne p-values give o3 significant in 4 of 7 scenarios and Claude-4-Thinking in 6 of 7 (25 iterations per condition, Mann-Whitney); FrameBench GPT-5 33.40% category change and 7.12% same-frame disagreement match (table rows are shifted in the PDF text but the prose agrees). FrameBench is a recommendation task rather than story format.

claim: Talboy and Fuller (2023) is a one-shot qualitative demonstration (three chatbots, one prompt per frame, two sessions) with no counts or percentages; no primary framing numbers exist in it.
agent_test: Do not cite it as a rate.

claim: Reasoning-trained open models resist attribute framing better than size-matched ordinary models (resistance score QwQ-32B .818 vs Qwen2.5-32B .602; R1-Qwen-14B .826 vs Qwen2.5-14B .365; R1-Llama-70B .717 vs Llama-3.3-70B .697). This sits against the 7-8B prompted-CoT result (28.6% to 57.1%).
agent_test: Toggle thinking on and off in the same frontier model on the same paired items.

claim: No study found tests these agent-relevant questions: (1) code-run canonical table vs self-rewrite vs instruction at equal tokens; (3) both wordings in one context for LLMs; (6) token budget and frame sensitivity; (7) votes with different canonical wordings vs same-wording sampling; (8) removing the zero outcome of the risky option in LLM prompts.
agent_test: Run the small experiment grid in critique.md (Gap search results) before building the S1 step.
